text:
ROXANE (standing near him):
  Each of us has a wound: I have mine.
  Still raw, it is there, that old wound,
  (She places her hand on her breast):
  It is there, beneath the letter with its yellowing paper,
  Where tears and blood can still be seen!
  (Twilight begins to fall.)

CYRANO:
  His letter! . . . Had you not said that one day, perhaps,
  You would let me read it?

ROXANE:
  Ah! you wish to? . . . His letter?

CYRANO:
  Yes. . . I wish to. . . Today. . .

ROXANE (giving him the pouch hanging from her neck):
  Here!

CYRANO (taking it):
  May I open it?

ROXANE:
  Open it. . . read! . . .
  (She returns to her embroidery frame, folds it up, and puts away her wool.)

CYRANO (reading):
  Roxane, farewell, I am going to die! . . .

ROXANE (stopping, astonished):
  Aloud?

CYRANO (reading):
  It is to be this evening, I think, my beloved!
  My soul is still heavy with unexpressed love,
  And I am dying! Never again, never will my intoxicated eyes,
  My gaze, whose. . .

ROXANE:
  How you read it,
  His letter!

CYRANO (continuing):
  . . .whose thrilling delight it was,
  Kiss in passing the gestures that you make;
  I see again a little one familiar to you,
  With which you touch your brow, and I should like to cry out. . .

ROXANE (disturbed):
  How you read it—this letter!
  (Night falls imperceptibly.)

CYRANO:
  And I cry:
  Farewell! . . .

ROXANE:
  You read it. . .

CYRANO:
  My dear one, my darling,
  My treasure. . .

ROXANE (dreamily):
  In a voice. . .

CYRANO:
  My love! . . .

ROXANE:
  In a voice. . .
  (She starts):
  But. . . which I am not hearing for the first time!
  (She approaches very softly, without his noticing, passes behind the armchair, bends over noiselessly, and looks at the letter.—The shadows deepen.)

CYRANO:
  My heart never left you for a single second,
  And I am and shall be, even in the other world,
  He who loved you beyond measure, he who. . .

ROXANE (placing her hand on his shoulder):
  How can you read now? It is dark.
  (He starts, turns, sees her there very close to him, makes a frightened gesture, and bows his head. A long silence. Then, in the now complete darkness, she speaks slowly, clasping her hands):
  And for fourteen years, he played this part:
  Being the old friend who comes to be amusing!

CYRANO:
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  No, no, Roxane, no!

ROXANE:
  I should have guessed when he spoke my name!

CYRANO:
  No, it was not I!

ROXANE:
  It was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you. . .

ROXANE:
  I see the whole generous imposture:
  The letters—it was you. . .

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The tender, wild words,
  It was you. . .

CYRANO:
  No!

ROXANE:
  The voice in the night—it was you!

CYRANO:
  I swear to you it was not!

ROXANE:
  The soul—it was yours!

CYRANO:
  I did not love you.

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (struggling):
  It was the other man!

ROXANE:
  You loved me!

CYRANO (in a weakening voice):
  No!

ROXANE:
  Already you say it more softly!

CYRANO:
  No, no, my dear love, I did not love you!

ROXANE:
  Ah! how many things have died. . . how many have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since upon this letter, in which he had no part,
  Those tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let this sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why? . . .
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau enter at a run.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was sure of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by thunder!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then. . . that weakness? . . . that? . . .

CYRANO:
  That is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  . . . And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac died by assassination.
  (He uncovers his head; it is seen to be wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head bandaged! . . .
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero with a sword thrust,
  To fall with its point in my heart!” . . .
  —Yes, that is what I used to say! . . . Fate is a mocker! . . .
  And here I am, killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  That is very good. I shall have failed at everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur! . . .

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not weep so loudly! . . .
  (He holds out his hand to him):
  What has become of you now, my fellow craftsman?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of. . . of. . . candles, at Molière’s theater.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am outraged! . . . Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  A whole one!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing? . . .”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from you!

CYRANO:
  Hush! hush! He did well! . . .
  (To Ragueneau):
  The scene has a great effect, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! They laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Was to be the one who prompts—and is forgotten!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! My whole life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadows,
  Others climbed up to gather glory’s kiss!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my grave:
  Molière has genius and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having rung, the nuns are seen passing at the back, along the path, on their way to the service):
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (restraining her):
  No! no! do not go and fetch anyone:
  By the time you returned, I should no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ is heard):
  I was lacking a little harmony. . . there it is.

ROXANE:
  I love you—live!
